flavor: They called themselves gods. Most of them died the way men do, and several of them died badly.
rules: Any Roman emperor, including usurpers who held real power and the Eastern emperors who ruled from Constantinople until 1453. A name that several emperors shared counts for the best known of them.

answers.lore: Rome's first emperor. The month of August is named after him.
Did not fiddle while Rome burned. The fiddle hadn't been invented.
Said to have planned to make his horse a consul, though the tale may be slander.
A philosopher-emperor whose private notebook, the Meditations, is still a bestseller.
Built a wall across Britain, and was the first emperor to wear a full beard.
Fought as a gladiator in the arena, and was strangled in his bath by a wrestler named Narcissus.
Split the empire in four, then retired to grow cabbages in what is now Croatia.
Gave citizenship to almost every free man in the empire, and built enormous baths.
The last emperor in the West, deposed in 476 as a teenager and pensioned off.
A teenage priest of a sun god, notorious for scandal. Murdered at eighteen.
Bought the throne at auction from the Praetorian Guard in 193. He lasted 66 days.
The first emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy, captured by the Persian king Shapur I in 260.
Called the Bulgar-Slayer. He ruled for almost 50 years, and never married.
The last Roman emperor. He died defending the walls of Constantinople in 1453.
Had his nose cut off when deposed, then came back and ruled again, some say with a golden one.
The first woman to rule the empire in her own right, from 797.
Ruled for about three weeks, at around eighty years old.
Justinian's formidable wife was an empress, not a ruler. A later Theodora did rule alone, in 1055.
Not the Great one: a Byzantine emperor who ruled alone from 912 and is said to have died of exhaustion after a game of polo.
A Gallic emperor of 269. Legend gives him a reign of two days; his coins suggest a few months.
A Gallic usurper of around 271, known from just two coins. One turned up in an Oxfordshire field in 2003.
Known only from gold coins found in Transylvania in 1713 and long dismissed as fakes. A 2022 study argued they are real.

traps.reason: Dictator for life, never emperor. His adopted heir, Augustus, was the first.
Triumvir, Cleopatra's lover, loser at Actium. Never emperor.
Caesar's great rival, never emperor.
A gladiator who led a slave revolt.
An orator and consul, murdered on Mark Antony's orders.
One of Caesar's assassins.
Crowned 'Emperor of the Romans' in 800, but by the Pope, founding a new Western line.
Queen of Egypt, never of Rome.
Queen of Palmyra, who defied Rome. Her son did claim the title, briefly.
Macedonian, and three centuries too early.
He fought the emperors. He wasn't one.
The general who deposed the last Western emperor, then ruled Italy as king, not emperor.
King of the Ostrogoths, who ruled Italy without the imperial title.
Justinian's great general, never emperor.
Dictator, not emperor.
The richest man in Rome, but never emperor.
An empress by marriage, never a ruler in her own right.
Queen of the Iceni, who burned Roman London.
Rome's greatest enemy, not its emperor.
A general and seven-time consul, never emperor.
Russell Crowe's general in Gladiator. Fiction.
One of Rome's legendary founders, never an emperor.
Augustus's general and right-hand man, never emperor.
A celebrated general and heir who died before he could rule.
Tiberius's ambitious prefect, who fell before he could rise further.
A general of the Republic, long before the emperors.
A senator of the Republic, never emperor.
Rome's last king, long before the emperors.
A governor of Judaea, never emperor.
Emperor of the French, not of the Romans.
A later Western line, crowned by popes from 800 on. The deep wants the older Rome.
A creature of fiction. Rome's real emperors were stranger.
Nero's tutor, never an emperor. His pupil ordered him to die.
A writer of Rome, not a ruler of it.
A client king in Judaea, ruling by Rome's leave. Never emperor.
The power behind a weak emperor's throne, never on it.
A title that grew from Caesar's own name, centuries on. Name one of the Romans who wore the original.
A title, not a man. Name one who held it.
He inherited the emperors' old priestly title, and their city, but not their throne.
Rome again, but two thousand years late.
A hero of the Republic, dead long before Rome had emperors.
The third man of the Second Triumvirate, pushed aside by Octavian. Never emperor.
An heir who died before he could rule.
Hadrian's beloved, made a god after he drowned in the Nile. Never an emperor.
More than one man. Name one of them.
A thing an emperor built, not the emperor. Name the man behind it.

source: Copied from the daily question "roman-emperors" on 28 November 2026.
